hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
hero.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an illegal medical spa from a shed in her backyard on Northwest Coosa Drive. The sentencing follows a multi-agency investigation that began in May 2025 when a victim reported partial facial paralysis after receiving Botox injections at Mena's makeshift business, Miracle Hand and Spa.

The victim received 62 units of Botox injections from Mena and later experienced partial facial paralysis. When confronted, Mena refunded the $325 payment and asked the victim to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the issues. When the paralysis persisted and the victim requested to see Mena's medical license, Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that investigators discovered had expired in February 2024. Mena also falsely claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

Port St. Lucie Police, working with PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health, executed a search warrant at Mena's residence in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox.

Mena was convicted on multiple charges including three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud for obtaining property valued at $300 or more, one count of fraud for obtaining property under $20,000, and one count of using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The victim had been referred to the illegal business by coworkers who had previously received services from Mena.

cards.headline: Federal Court Blocks Florida Enforcement Lawsuit Against Pediatricians Over Gender Care Advocacy
cards.body:
A federal court in Illinois has granted a preliminary injunction blocking Florida from pursuing an enforcement lawsuit against the American Academy of Pediatrics, dealing a significant blow to the state's efforts to penalize the medical organization for its support of gender-affirming care for transgender youth. The injunction halts Attorney General James Uthmeier's lawsuit, which accused the nonprofit pediatricians organization of deceptive trade practices, racketeering, and antitrust violations based on its medical guidance and policy advocacy.

The federal court found the academy plausibly demonstrated that Florida filed the lawsuit to punish and suppress its protected speech. In granting the injunction, the court determined that the Florida complaint contains significant misrepresentations of the academy's policy statements and rests on a weak legal theory that its medical guidance constituted commercial speech. The court concluded the state appears to have brought the case in bad faith without a reasonable expectation of success on the merits.

The ruling represents a major development in the ongoing legal and political battle over transgender healthcare in Florida. The American Academy of Pediatrics, a national organization representing pediatricians, has publicly supported gender-affirming care for transgender youth as medically appropriate treatment. Florida officials have taken an aggressive stance against such care, and the enforcement lawsuit represented an attempt to use consumer protection and antitrust laws to challenge medical organizations that advocate for treatment policies at odds with state positions.

The preliminary injunction means Florida cannot proceed with its enforcement action while the underlying case continues in federal court. The decision raises questions about whether other states might face similar legal obstacles if they attempt to use enforcement powers against medical organizations based on their advocacy and clinical guidance. The case highlights the intersection of free speech protections, medical professional standards, and state regulatory authority. The American Academy of Pediatrics can continue its advocacy and policy work without facing immediate legal consequences from Florida during the litigation.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce coral reef protections rolled back as activists rally to save rare deep-sea ecosystem
cards.body:
A federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found only off the coast of Fort Pierce. The reef sits hundreds of feet below the surface and is home to more than 2,000 marine species. Unlike most coral that requires shallow sunlight, the Oculina Bank thrives in deep, dark waters.

Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County to rally support for preserving the reef. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who has dived the rare reef, warned that the ecosystem depends on the coral's habitat. "Very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food," Gilmore said. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish."

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were established decades ago. The proposals followed a Trump Executive order issued in April 2025 that directed eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, believes reopening shrimping access is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. "The shrimping industry is teetering on the brink of extinction," Zales said.

Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers dropped from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, with just 12 active boats in 2018. Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, and other scientists urged the public to help save the reef. "Corals are in trouble worldwide. We shouldn't be destroying anymore," Gilmore said. The reef's corals grow very slowly and have existed for a long time, making recovery from damage extremely difficult.

cards.headline: Martin County Sheriff arrests three in theft ring that hit 40 hardware stores across Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: Three men have been arrested in connection with Operation Hammer Time, a retail theft ring that burglarized more than 40 hardware stores across 13 counties, including multiple locations in Stuart, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter.
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a large-scale retail theft operation dubbed Operation Hammer Time. Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31, are accused of participating in a series of burglaries at hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach, and St. Lucie counties from December 2025 to April 2026. Major Ruben Romero said at least 40 stores across 13 counties were burglarized, with stolen goods transported back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be resold.

Investigators said roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage caused to the stores. Hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce, and Jupiter were targeted, along with stores in Broward County. According to a Martin County Sheriff's Office affidavit, the crews used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash glass doors and complete the thefts within minutes, often before police could arrive or alarms were triggered. Batista is connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025.

Aldana-Ferrera is currently in custody in Georgia, Batista was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and is being held in Martin County Jail, and Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. Romero noted the impact of these thefts extends beyond the immediate losses, saying the more they steal and the more damage they cause, the more expensive things become for residents. The suspects face charges including racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure, and burglary of an unoccupied structure.

cards.headline: Florida legislature approves expanded homestead property tax exemption, sends constitutional amendment to voters
cards.body:
The Florida legislature has approved a measure to expand the homestead property tax exemption and will place a constitutional amendment on the ballot for voters to decide. The proposal represents a significant change to property tax policy that could affect homeowners across the Treasure Coast and throughout the state.

The legislation moves forward amid ongoing debate about property tax relief and its impact on local government revenues. Property taxes fund essential county and municipal services including schools, law enforcement, fire protection, and infrastructure maintenance in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

The constitutional amendment will require voter approval before taking effect. Constitutional amendments in Florida need 60 percent support from voters to pass. The measure is part of broader discussions in Tallahassee about property tax reform as homeowners across Florida have faced rising property values and corresponding tax bills.

Voters will see the amendment on an upcoming ballot. Local government officials and school districts will be watching closely, as changes to the homestead exemption directly affect how much property tax revenue counties and municipalities collect to fund public services. The expanded exemption would reduce the taxable value of primary residences for eligible homeowners.

cards.headline: Multi-county retail theft ring hit 40 stores including Stuart hardware shops, Martin County Sheriff reports
cards.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a coordinated retail theft ring that targeted hardware stores across the Treasure Coast and beyond. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31 were involved in a series of burglaries at hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties from December 2025 to April 2026. The operation, dubbed Operation Hammer Time, saw at least 40 stores burglarized across 13 counties.

According to the sheriff's office, the thieves used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash glass doors and windows at hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce and Jupiter, as well as locations in Broward County. The crews completed thefts within minutes, often before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Investigators say the stolen merchandise was transported back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage caused to the stores.

Batista, connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025, was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, while Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. Romero said there are burglaries that happened before December, and investigators are still looking for one other suspect.

The suspects face charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero highlighted the broader community impact, noting that retail theft contributes to higher prices. "There's already inflation that we notice severely in our state, and the more they steal, the more damage they cause, the more expensive things are," Romero said. "People can't go to work because they can't afford the tools."

cards.headline: Florida lawmakers pass $200,000 homestead tax exemption increase requiring voter approval
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut proposal Tuesday that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years. The measure needs approval from 60% of voters in November.
cards.body:
Florida lawmakers on Tuesday passed a property tax cut proposal that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The bill would still need approval from 60% of voters in November. The measure would also lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10% to 5%.

Experts are divided on the potential consequences of the proposed tax cut. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace, based in Boynton Beach, raised the possibility of new fees tied to local services. "There could potentially be non-ad valorem taxes assigned to the sheriff's office, fire rescue, some of the other things. Additionally, there may be some increased fees because the only other way that the county or the local governments can derive revenue," Wallace said. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could end up carrying more of the financial burden to offset lost revenue.

Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi offered a different perspective, suggesting the measure could push home prices higher. "I expect home prices could actually increase because now home buyers have more money at their disposal, and that in the past has resulted in home prices going up," Gastesi said. Realtor Danielle Blake was skeptical of that theory, pointing to interest rates as a more significant barrier to sales than property taxes alone. All four experts acknowledged significant unknowns about how counties, municipalities and markets might respond to decreasing property tax revenue. If the ballot measure passes, lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee to work out the specifics in a bill to implement the changes.

cards.headline: Five hospitalized after multi-vehicle crash sparks fire on I-95 in Stuart
cards.teaser: Five people were taken to hospitals Monday night after a multi-vehicle collision on Interstate 95 northbound near Exit 101 that caused one vehicle to catch fire.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue responded to a multi-vehicle crash on Interstate 95 northbound near Exit 101 and Halpatiokee Regional Park just before 10 p.m. Monday. When crews arrived, they found one of the vehicles on fire and quickly extinguished the flames. Two people suffered traumatic injuries and were transported to the hospital, while three others sustained minor injuries and were also taken for medical treatment.

All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed while law enforcement investigated the crash scene. As of Tuesday morning, all lanes had reopened to traffic. The Florida Highway Patrol is conducting the investigation into the cause of the collision.

The crash occurred on a heavily traveled stretch of I-95 in Martin County, creating significant delays for northbound motorists during the evening hours. The area near Exit 101 provides access to Halpatiokee Regional Park and surrounding Stuart neighborhoods.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman loses home and son's photos after lightning strike sparks fire
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera returned from getting a haircut at church last month to find her Fort Pierce home destroyed by a lightning strike fire, leaving her displaced and without insurance.
cards.body:
A utility worker stopped Rosa Rivera outside her Fort Pierce home last month with devastating news: her house was on fire. St. Lucie County Fire District firefighters rushed to extinguish the flames, which were caused by a lightning strike. Rivera, who had been getting a haircut at church, returned to find her home heavily damaged with broken windows and destruction throughout.

Rivera lost clothes, furniture, and irreplaceable personal belongings, including photographs of her late son who passed away three years ago. The damage left Rivera displaced and she is now staying at her nephew's home while she works to rebuild. Rivera is uninsured and was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home, making the situation even more difficult to manage.

Despite the overwhelming losses, Rivera expressed gratitude that she was not home when the lightning strike occurred. A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild her life and home.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted swimming through Port St. Lucie's Town Park neighborhood
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie police shared rare video of a black bear swimming through a residential waterway in the Town Park community before exiting and running toward nearby homes.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police released video footage Tuesday showing a large black bear navigating through residential waters in the Town Park community before exiting and running toward nearby homes. The unusual wildlife sighting was described by officials as seasonal behavior for Florida's black bear population, which becomes more active this time of year while searching for food. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission Bear Management Program said they are monitoring the bear and may set a trap to capture and relocate it if the animal does not move from the area on its own.

Bear sightings remain rare throughout most of the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County regions, making Tuesday's Port St. Lucie encounter particularly noteworthy for local residents. Wildlife officials recommend residents maintain significant distance from bears, never approach the animals, and avoid any attempts to feed them. Port St. Lucie police advise keeping children and pets away from bears and securing potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around properties.

Florida's black bear population has grown substantially in recent years following decades of conservation efforts after the species was once listed as threatened. During unexpected bear encounters, officials stress remaining calm, avoiding running, slowly backing away while keeping the bear visible, speaking in calm firm tones, and ensuring the animal has a clear escape route.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff swears in 12 Make-A-Wish children as junior deputies
cards.teaser: Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro on Wednesday, including twins where one donated bone marrow to save the other.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office honored 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation on Wednesday when Sheriff Richard Del Toro swore them in as junior deputies. Among the newest junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder, and needed a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save his sister's life, enduring time in a wheelchair and significant pain during the process.

Another junior deputy, Tobias Deleon, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity Deleon said things that do not normally happen to a child happened to him, and at one point they even lost him before medical teams were able to bring him back and he miraculously recovered. During the ceremony, the junior deputies received badges, toured the sheriff's office, and saw demonstrations by the helicopter, SWAT team, and K-9 units.

Sheriff Del Toro called it one of the greatest days in his career and thanked the children for making the department's wish come true. The mothers expressed gratitude for the sheriff's office taking the time and energy to welcome their children into the community and remind them they are important.

cards.headline: Historic Boston House in Fort Pierce reopens as downtown dining destination
cards.teaser: The Boston House, a Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, has reopened as a new restaurant honoring the building's history while bringing fresh energy downtown.
cards.body:
The Boston House, a historic Fort Pierce landmark built in 1909 along South Indian River Drive, has officially reopened as a new dining experience. The home is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served various roles over the decades. The newest owners are working to preserve its past while reimagining its purpose for modern use. Co-owner Georgette Angelos said she wants guests to feel at home automatically while honoring the building's legacy.

Originally built by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, the Boston House remains closely tied to the region's early development. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past. Each room in the Boston House offers a distinct experience rooted in local history, blending preservation with a modern dining atmosphere.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown, noting that Fort Pierce has done a great job bringing new life to the downtown area. The reopening represents both the preservation of an important historic structure and a renewed gathering place for the community as downtown Fort Pierce continues its revitalization efforts.

hero.body:

The Cresswind project is a residential development that will now fall under Sebastian's jurisdiction for planning, zoning, and municipal services. The annexation process had been underway as the city worked to incorporate the development into its official boundaries.

The finalized annexation means Sebastian will provide city services to the development and collect property taxes from the area. This type of annexation is common when new residential communities are built adjacent to existing city boundaries.

The completion of the Cresswind annexation marks another step in Sebastian's ongoing growth and development along the Treasure Coast. The city has been evaluating various annexation proposals as residential development continues in Indian River County.

An heiress is using her wealth to protect natural areas in Hobe Sound by purchasing land that might otherwise be developed. She has acquired property adjacent to the Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve and donated it to conservation efforts.

The land purchases represent a private conservation strategy to prevent Florida development from encroaching on sensitive natural areas. By buying parcels near the existing preserve, the donor can ensure the land remains in its natural state rather than being converted to residential or commercial use.

The Hobe Sound Scrub Preserve is an important protected area in Martin County, home to rare scrub habitat and endangered species. The additional donated land will help buffer and expand the preserve, protecting more of the unique coastal scrub ecosystem found in this part of the Treasure Coast.

cards.body:
Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong beach celebration as more than 100 paddlers complete an 80-mile open ocean journey from Bimini, Bahamas. The endurance athletes will launch at midnight and paddle for 12 to 16 hours as part of the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis, arriving at Lake Worth Beach sometime during the day.

Event founder Travis Suit established the crossing and the Pipers Angels Foundation in honor of his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. Suit, an avid paddler, was inspired to create the event after learning about the natural respiratory benefits of ocean salt air. Participants must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, with crew and virtual participants committing to a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. Participants will take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner on Thursday, followed by a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony on Friday to honor cystic fibrosis warriors. Safety requirements are strict, with all paddlers required to wear Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, reflective gear during dark hours, and GPS trackers that must remain active throughout the journey. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

hero.headline: Federal Court Blocks Florida Enforcement Lawsuit Against Pediatricians Over Gender Care Advocacy
hero.body:
A federal court in Illinois has granted a preliminary injunction blocking Florida from pursuing an enforcement lawsuit against the American Academy of Pediatrics, dealing a significant blow to the state's efforts to penalize the medical organization for its support of gender-affirming care for transgender youth. The injunction halts Attorney General James Uthmeier's lawsuit, which accused the nonprofit pediatricians organization of deceptive trade practices, racketeering, and antitrust violations based on its medical guidance and policy advocacy.

The federal court found the academy plausibly demonstrated that Florida filed the lawsuit to punish and suppress its protected speech. In granting the injunction, the court determined that the Florida complaint contains significant misrepresentations of the academy's policy statements and rests on a weak legal theory that its medical guidance constituted commercial speech. The court concluded the state appears to have brought the case in bad faith without a reasonable expectation of success on the merits.

The ruling represents a major development in the ongoing legal and political battle over transgender healthcare in Florida. The American Academy of Pediatrics, a national organization representing pediatricians, has publicly supported gender-affirming care for transgender youth as medically appropriate treatment. Florida officials have taken an aggressive stance against such care, and the enforcement lawsuit represented an attempt to use consumer protection and antitrust laws to challenge medical organizations that advocate for treatment policies at odds with state positions.

The preliminary injunction means Florida cannot proceed with its enforcement action while the underlying case continues in federal court. The decision raises questions about whether other states might face similar legal obstacles if they attempt to use enforcement powers against medical organizations based on their advocacy and clinical guidance. The case highlights the intersection of free speech protections, medical professional standards, and state regulatory authority. The American Academy of Pediatrics can continue its advocacy and policy work without facing immediate legal consequences from Florida during the litigation.

hero.headline: Multi-county retail theft ring hit 40 stores including Stuart hardware shops, Martin County Sheriff reports
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced arrests in a coordinated retail theft ring that targeted hardware stores across the Treasure Coast and beyond. Major Ruben Romero said Johnny Batista, 19, Roberto Hernandez-Castro, 39, and Roberto Aldana-Ferrera, 31 were involved in a series of burglaries at hardware stores across Martin, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties from December 2025 to April 2026. The operation, dubbed Operation Hammer Time, saw at least 40 stores burglarized across 13 counties.

According to the sheriff's office, the thieves used sledgehammers or other blunt objects to smash glass doors and windows at hardware stores in Stuart, Lake Worth, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach, West Palm Beach, Fort Pierce and Jupiter, as well as locations in Broward County. The crews completed thefts within minutes, often before police arrived or alarms were triggered. Investigators say the stolen merchandise was transported back to Miami-Dade County, where the suspects lived, to be sold. Roughly $500,000 worth of property was stolen, in addition to damage caused to the stores.

Batista, connected to the first known theft at Sewell Hardware in Stuart in December 2025, was arrested in February for a vehicle theft and remains in Martin County Jail. Aldana-Ferrera is in custody in Georgia, while Hernandez-Castro has a warrant out for his arrest. A fourth suspect, Maikell Fleitas, is deceased. Romero said there are burglaries that happened before December, and investigators are still looking for one other suspect.

The suspects face charges of racketeering, burglary over $1,000 in damage while masked, burglary of an occupied structure and burglary of an unoccupied structure. Romero highlighted the broader community impact, noting that retail theft contributes to higher prices. cards.headline: Martin County residents rally at Blake Library to save rare deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth.
cards.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County after a federally appointed council voted to roll back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth. Located just off the coast of Fort Pierce, the reef is hidden hundreds of feet below the surface and thrives in deep, dark waters unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive. The reef is home to more than 2,000 marine species.

Scientists Dr. Grant Gilmore and Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, urged the public to help save the reef at the gathering. Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. "Very concerned about an ecosystem point of view, where your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food," Gilmore said. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish."

The proposals followed an executive order issued in April 2025 that tasked eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate the fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, believes reopening shrimping access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers dropped from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, with just 12 active boats in 2018.

Residents should keep children and pets away from bears and secure potential food sources including garbage, pet food, and bird seed around their properties.

cards.headline: 12 Make-A-Wish children sworn in as junior deputies at St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office
cards.teaser: Sheriff Richard Del Toro honored 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation in a special swearing-in ceremony, calling it one of the greatest days in his career.
cards.body:
Twelve kids from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro on Wednesday. The children received badges, toured the sheriff's office, and saw demonstrations from the helicopter, SWAT team and K-9 units. Del Toro called it one of the greatest days in his career.

Among the newest junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder, and needed a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save his sister's life, enduring a wheelchair and significant pain during the process. Mia said her brother made her feel safe during the frightening experience.

Another junior deputy, Tobias Deleon, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity Deleon said things that don't normally happen to a child happened to him, and they even lost him at one point before doctors were able to bring him back and he miraculously recovered. She thanked the sheriff's office for making the time and energy to welcome the children into the community and remind them that they're important. Sheriff Del Toro said the children left an imprint on the department, telling them they made the sheriff's office's wish come true.

The building was originally constructed by an engineer for Henry Flagler's Florida East Coast Railway, who later became St. Lucie County's third sheriff, tying the structure closely to the region's early development. Co-owner Georgette Angelos said the goal is to make guests feel at home while honoring the building's legacy. During renovations, the owners intentionally preserved historic details, including low original ceilings and Florida-themed law books that nod to the home's past.

General manager Scott Laird said the revival of the property reflects broader momentum downtown. cards.headline: Fort Pierce woman displaced after lightning strike destroys home, loses irreplaceable photos of late son
cards.teaser: Rosa Rivera lost clothes, furniture and irreplaceable personal belongings including photos of her late son when lightning struck her Fort Pierce home last month, causing a fire.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce woman is displaced and calling for help after a lightning strike tore through her home last month, leaving her with broken windows, heavy damage, and almost nothing left. Rosa Rivera returned home from getting a haircut at church when a utility worker stopped her outside. The utility worker told her he thought her house was on fire. St. Lucie County District Firefighters rushed to put out the flames, and Rivera was told a lightning strike caused the fire.

Walking into her damaged home left Rivera stunned. She lost clothes, furniture and irreplaceable personal belongings including photos of her late son, who passed away three years ago. The damage left Rivera displaced. She is uninsured and is now staying at her nephew's home while she rebuilds. Rivera, who is also disabled, was recovering from neck fusion surgery the same week she lost her home.

A memorial outside the damaged home is one of the few things Rivera has left that cannot be replaced. Despite everything, Rivera said she is holding onto gratitude that she was not inside when the fire broke out. It's a blessing that I was not home, she said, and I was in a safe place instead of being at home to where something could've possibly happened to me. A GoFundMe has been set up to help Rivera rebuild.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.teaser: Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St.
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an illegal medical spa called Miracle Hand and Spa out of a shed in her backyard. The case began in May 2025 when a victim reported to police that she experienced partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections from Mena at the makeshift facility in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. The victim, who had been referred by coworkers who previously used Mena's services, paid $325 for the procedure.

After the victim reported the paralysis to Mena, she received a refund but was asked to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the problems. When the paralysis continued, the victim requested to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered certificate of phlebotomy that had actually expired in February 2024, according to the agency that issued it. Mena also claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic in an attempt to reassure the victim.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives discovered an extensive operation including medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines and injection devices for fillers and Botox.

Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of health safety practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud-swindle obtain property $300 or more, one count of fraud-swindle obtain property under $20,000 and one count of use of two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The case underscores the dangers of unlicensed medical procedures and the importance of verifying credentials before receiving cosmetic treatments.
